record_type_quote: Following that logic, we re-analyzed data from one previous study (Nosek & Smyth, 2011) and replicated another (Lane et al., 2012) to examine what happens to the advantage of the gender-science IAT over self-report measures in predicting a science-relevant outcome, when attitudes are added to the model.

targets.authors: Lane, K. A., Goh, J. X., & Driver-Linn, E.
targets.title: Implicit science stereotypes mediate the relationship between gender and academic participation.
targets.evidence_quote: Lane et al. (2012) found that the gender-science IAT predicted students' plans to pursue science versus humanities (r = .34, p < .0001) better than the self-reported stereotype (r = .12, ns), Williams' t(150) = 2.158, p = .03. We repeated that study with similar materials and procedure, adding attitude and importance measures, measured and scored identically to our main present study (full details about the replication are in Appendix C, and at osf.io/vc68r).
targets.outcome_quote: Importantly, we did not find evidence that the IAT maintained its advantage over the explicit stereotypes after controlling for attitudes. When we partialled out shared variance with attitudes, the IAT/pursuit relation (r = .095, p = .032) was no longer reliably stronger than the explicit stereotype/pursuit relation (r = .019, p = .662), Williams' t(511) = 1.251, p = .212.
targets.outcome_reasoning: The original advantage is obtained, but the central message is that the implicit/explicit contrast does not isolate the proposed construct: controlling personal attitudes removes reliable evidence for the IAT advantage. The restricted freshmen analysis fails, but the authors attribute that exploratory subset result to random error.

targets.authors: Nosek, B. A., & Smyth, F. L.
targets.title: Implicit social cognitions predict sex differences in math engagement and achievement.
targets.evidence_quote: Nosek and Smyth (2011) compared the gender-science IAT and the explicit stereotype (measured with two self-reported items: Men are better at math than women are and Women can achieve as much as men in math) in predicting math-related outcomes. We re-analyzed that data and found only one variable, the difference between math and verbal SAT scores, that had reliably stronger relation with the IAT (r = .193, p < .001) than the explicit stereotype (r = .090, p = .004), Williams' t(1040) = 2.590, p = .010.
targets.outcome_computational_quote: To refute that possibility, we returned to previous research that found an advantage of the IAT, and tested whether the evidence for this advantage persists even when controlling for self-reported liking.
targets.outcome_robustness_quote: Importantly, when we computed partial correlations between each measure and the SAT, partialling out shared variance with attitudes, there was no longer reliable evidence for an IAT advantage: The IAT/SAT relation (r =.049, p = .115) was not significantly better than the explicit stereotype/SAT relation (r = .017, p = .584), Williams' t(1040) < 1, p = .442.
targets.outcome_reasoning: Analysis directly tests a covariate-adjusted specification; it does not report an audit of recovery of original numerical results. The IAT advantage disappears with attitude adjustment.

reasoning: Mixed design: a new-sample replication of Lane et al. and an original-data reanalysis of Nosek and Smyth. Target-specific reproduction axes retain the latter. Main archival analysis and background citations are not additional targets.
